title: De quibusdam eximiis proprietatibus circa divisores potestatum occurrentibus

deep.reconstruction:
Context. In this part of the paper Euler studies, for a prime P = 4n-1, the numbers p = n + q^2 + q (q = 0, 1, 2, ...). Since 4p = P + (2q+1)^2, we have 4p ≡ (2q+1)^2 (mod P). So every p is a quadratic residue mod P. The 'residua simplicia' r are the primes (and 1) that occur as factors of the p.

Example 14 (P = 103, n = 26). The values 26 + q^2 + q for q = 0..9 are 26, 28, 32, 38, 46, 56, 68, 82, 98, 116. These factor as 2·13, 2^2·7, 2^5, 2·19, 2·23, 2^3·7, 2^2·17, 2·41, 2·7^2, 2^2·29. The prime factors found are r = 1, 2, 7, 13, 17, 19, 23, 29, 41, and all of them are indeed quadratic residues mod 103.

§20 (Scholion), first observation. Every prime occurring in some p is itself a residue mod P.

§20, second observation. A small prime l appears in the whole sequence only if it already appears among the first (l+1)/2 terms:
- 2 appears only if n is even;
- 3 only within the first 2 terms;
- 5 within the first 3;
- 7 within the first 4.
The reason is that q(q+1) mod l depends only on q mod l and is invariant under q -> -1-q. Euler suggests this observation 'might lead to a demonstration'.

§20, warning about composite 4n-1. He shows with n = 30 (4n-1 = 119 = 7·17) that the property fails or at least cannot be inferred. The p-values are 30, 32, 36, 42, 50, 60, 72, 86, 102, 120, 140, 162. The factor 2 is a residue (2 is a square mod 7 and mod 17). After removing it, the remaining parts are 15, 9, 21, 25, 43, 51, 35, 81, and no conclusion about 3, 5, 7 is possible: products of two non-residues are residues. In fact 3 and 5 are non-residues mod both 7 and 17. So 3 has Jacobi symbol +1 mod 119 without being a residue; this is exactly the Jacobi-symbol caveat.

§21 (Conclusio). If P = 4n-1 is prime, then all prime factors of all n + q^2 + q are quadratic residues mod P. In modern terms: a prime l with l | (2q+1)^2 + P has (-P/l) = 1. Quadratic reciprocity, with P ≡ 3 (mod 4), turns this into (l/P) = 1. For l = 2: p ≡ n (mod 2), so 2 | p iff P ≡ 7 (mod 8), when 2 is a residue. So the Conclusio is an equivalent form of (part of) quadratic reciprocity, stated inductively, not proved.

§22 (Theorema generale). Let T = (2q+1)^2 - 4at. If P = 4as + T or P = 4as - T is prime, then a is a quadratic residue mod P.
- First case: P = 4a(s-t) + (2q+1)^2, so P - (2q+1)^2 = 4a(s-t). By the companion results for primes 4n+1 (treated earlier in the paper), the corresponding p is ±a(s-t).
- Second case: P = 4a(s+t) - (2q+1)^2, so P + (2q+1)^2 = 4a(s+t), giving p = a(s+t) = n + q^2 + q.
- In both cases a divides p, so every prime factor of a is a residue, and hence a is a residue.
This is Euler's classical formulation of quadratic reciprocity: a is a QR mod a prime P whenever P ≡ ±(odd square) (mod 4a). The next page draws the corollary that a^m ≡ 1 mod 2m+1 (Euler's criterion) and counts the classes of T mod 4a.
errors: The demonstration of §22 rests entirely on the unproved Conclusio of §21 (and its 4n+1 analogue), i.e. on quadratic reciprocity itself; it is a reduction, not a proof.
In the case P = 4as+T, Euler writes p = a(s-t) without regard to sign. For P ≡ 1 mod 4 the natural quantity is q^2+q-n = -a(s-t); this is harmless since -1 is a residue, but it is unstated.
The tacit conditions gcd(a,P) = 1 and P not dividing the relevant p are not mentioned.
The remark that 'hence 119 is not prime' is not a deduction from the list; Euler simply notes the composite case.

ideas.what: Prime factors of n+q^2+q are quadratic residues mod the prime 4n-1
ideas.modern_name: Quadratic reciprocity (in the form: l | x^2+P implies (l/P)=1 for P≡3 mod 4), including the supplementary law for 2
ideas.where_published: E552 'Observationes circa divisionem quadratorum per numeros primos' (Opusc. anal. I, 1783); earlier E164 and related papers

ideas.what: A prime l occurs among all values of n+q(q+1) iff it occurs among the first (l+1)/2 values, by periodicity and q -> -1-q symmetry
ideas.modern_name: Periodicity of quadratic polynomials mod l / representability of residues by x^2+x+n

ideas.what: For composite modulus 119, a number may have all 'Jacobi-type' indications of residuacity yet fail to be a residue (products of two non-residues)
ideas.modern_name: Jacobi symbol +1 vs. genuine quadratic residue for composite moduli

ideas.what: a is a QR mod any prime P ≡ ±T (mod 4a), with T an odd square minus a multiple of 4a
ideas.modern_name: Euler's form of the quadratic reciprocity law
ideas.where_published: E552 and E557 (Opuscula analytica I, 1783); discussed by Weil, Lemmermeyer 'Reciprocity Laws'

missed.claim: Euler suggests that the 'small primes appear early' periodicity observation might yield a proof of the Conclusio (reciprocity). The idea is a descent/induction on the size of prime factors, never carried out by him. It is close in spirit to Gauss's first (inductive) proof, but too vague to count as new.
missed.quote: quae obseruatio fortasse ad demonstrationem deducere posset
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historically only: a hint of an inductive proof strategy for reciprocity predating Gauss; of marginal interest given existing historiography.

deep.surprise_reason: The page states Euler's well-known formulation of quadratic reciprocity (already documented from E552/E557). The 119 example neatly illustrates the Jacobi-symbol pitfall, and Euler hints at an inductive proof idea. Both are minor and broadly covered in histories of reciprocity.
transcription_corrections: In the n=30 list, '2^3.3.5[?]' should read 2^3.3.5 (= 120, the value for q=9); the bracketed query should be removed.
'2.9^2' is correct as printed (=162 = 2·3^4), matching '3^4' in the reduced list.
